title: Jonah sulks (Jonah 4)
hook: angry at God's mercy, Jonah mourns a shady plant; God asks: shouldn't I pity Nineveh?
carry: mercy is wider than you like

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nineveh turns, from the king down to the cattle. Your line was even nineveh. When you caught yourself writing someone off, did you manage to ask, who can tell? Day four hundred eighty-eight.

If the book of Jonah were a movie, it would end after chapter three. The city repents, God relents, roll credits. But there's a fourth chapter, and it opens with the prophet furious. In the King James Bible: "But it displeased Jonah exceedingly, and he was very angry." He has just watched a whole city turn at five words, and he's livid. And then he finally tells God why he ran in the first place. It wasn't fear of the storm, or fear of the Assyrians. It was something much more uncomfortable. He was afraid God would be kind.

Here's Jonah's complaint, and it sounds almost like a hymn: "I knew that thou art a gracious God, and merciful, slow to anger, and of great kindness." Those words echo God's own self-description to Moses on the mountain in Exodus. Jonah knows the creed by heart. He just hates that it applies to Nineveh. So he asks to die, and God answers with a short, gentle question: "Doest thou well to be angry?" Jonah doesn't reply. He walks out east of the city, builds a little shelter, and sits to see what will become of it. Then the comic part. God makes a leafy plant grow up overnight to shade his head. The King James calls it a gourd; nobody is quite sure what plant the Hebrew word means. And Jonah, the text says, "was exceeding glad of the gourd." The one time the book calls him glad, it's over shade. Next morning, God sends a worm, the plant withers, the sun beats down and a hot east wind blows, and Jonah wants to die again, this time over a plant. And God makes his point: you pitied a plant you didn't plant or grow, which came up in a night and died in a night. Should I not pity Nineveh, that great city, with more than a hundred and twenty thousand people who can't tell their right hand from their left, and also much cattle? And that's where the book ends. On a question. We never hear Jonah's answer. Some readers hear that silence as an invitation: the answer is left to them. And notice the last words in English: much cattle. God's mercy, in this book, reaches even the cows.
screen: `GLAD OF A GOURD, THEN A WORM.`
then, large: `SHOULD NOT I SPARE NINEVEH?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice when mercy annoys you. Settle, and breathe. Think of a time someone got off easy and it bothered you. A coworker who wasn't fired. A sibling who was forgiven too fast. A public figure who got a second chance you didn't think they deserved. Let the irritation come up, and don't judge it. Jonah felt it too, and the book doesn't pretend otherwise. Then hear God's question, as gently as it's asked in the story: is it right for you to be angry? You don't have to answer. Just sit with it. If you pray, you can bring your irritation to God honestly, the way Jonah did. If you don't, simply notice where it lives in your body. The bell holds the time.
Jonah sulks. Angry that God spared his enemies, glad of a shady plant, and left facing a question the book never lets him answer.

Your line: mercy is wider than you like. Today, when someone else gets grace you think they haven't earned, try not to grumble out loud. Just notice the sulk, and smile at it. Day four hundred eighty-eight.

howItsDone: Some Christians read Jonah 4 alongside Jesus's parable of the prodigal son, where the older brother also resents a welcome; sermons pair them to ask how people respond to mercy shown to others.

fork.setup: you're Jonah. your enemies were spared, your shade plant just died, and God asks: is it right for you to be angry? what does the book say you answer?
options: yes, I'm right to be angry.
fork.reveal: the book ends on God's question about Nineveh and much cattle. Jonah's answer is left blank, and some readers hear it as theirs to give.

original.note: Hebrew: gracious. the first word of God's description in Jonah's complaint, the creed he knew by heart, and resented.

trapdoor: what you thought: Jonah obeyed in the end, so the story's over.
what it means: the prophet is angry that God is merciful to his enemies, and God answers with a plant, a worm and a question.
what a scholar hears: Jonah's complaint quotes God's self-description in Exodus 34:6, turned into an accusation.

notes: 'More than sixscore thousand persons' (4:11) rendered as 'more than a hundred and twenty thousand people'. Confirm.
The Hebrew qiqayon is of uncertain identity (castor-oil plant is a common guess; Jerome rendered it 'ivy', which famously caused controversy). Kept to 'nobody is quite sure'.
The last word of the book in Hebrew is behemah rabbah ('much cattle'); in English the KJV also ends 'and also much cattle?'. Confirm the match item.
Jonah's anger is about God's mercy to Nineveh; the script avoids implying anything about Jewish attitudes generally.
Prodigal son pairing in howItsDone is a common preaching connection; confirm.

Editor pass (y2 review): 'the last word is cattle' is true only in English (the Hebrew ends on rabbah, 'much'); now 'the last words in English: much cattle', and the match pair follows. The original note called chanun the creed's first word, but Exodus 34:6 begins with rachum; now 'first word in Jonah's complaint' (4:2). 'Hoping for fire' replaced with the text's 'to see what would become of the city' (4:5). 'Most successful sermon in the Bible' and 'happiest in the whole book' superlatives removed; 'Christians have often' softened.
